healthInfo.emergencyNumber: 112 (EU emergency), 112 (also connects to INEM ambulance service), 111 (medical helpline for non-emergencies)
healthInfo.qualityNotes: Good healthcare system with modern facilities, particularly in Lisbon, Porto, and the Algarve. English is commonly spoken in tourist areas and private healthcare. Public healthcare is accessible but can have longer wait times. Many private hospitals and clinics cater to tourists.
healthInfo.pharmacyHours: Most pharmacies open 9am-7pm weekdays, with reduced hours on weekends. In every area, one pharmacy stays open 24/7 or for extended hours — look for the green cross sign or ask any pharmacy for the nearest 'farmácia de serviço/noturno' (on-duty pharmacy).
healthInfo.pharmacyTips: Pharmacies (farmácia) are very accessible and pharmacists are helpful. Many medications require a prescription. Portugal has a strong pharmacy culture — pharmacists can advise on minor ailments and some medications are available without prescription.
healthInfo.prescriptionRules: EU prescriptions are accepted. Non-EU prescriptions require validation by a Portuguese doctor. Many medications that are OTC in some countries require prescriptions here.

restrictedMeds.name: Codeine-containing medications
restrictedMeds.note: Codeine products require a prescription in Portugal. Some codeine products may be restricted.

restrictedMeds.name: ADHD medications (Adderall, Ritalin, methylphenidate)
restrictedMeds.note: Controlled substances. A Portuguese prescription or special authorization is required.

restrictedMeds.name: Benzodiazepines
restrictedMeds.note: Controlled substances requiring a prescription. Portugal has strict regulations.

restrictedMeds.name: Medical cannabis
restrictedMeds.note: Medical cannabis is legal in Portugal for specific conditions. THC/cannabis products remain heavily restricted.

healthInfo.bringDocumentation: Carry a doctor's letter and prescription (ideally in Portuguese or English) for all medications. Bring sufficient supply in original packaging. For controlled substances, carry prescription documentation. EU citizens should carry the EHIC/GHIC card.

travelInsurance.requiredNote: Not legally required for short stays, but strongly recommended. EU citizens should carry EHIC/GHIC.
travelInsurance.tips: INEM (national emergency service) provides free emergency medical care. Private hospitals and clinics are excellent but require payment or insurance guarantee upfront. Travel insurance with medical evacuation coverage is recommended.

vaccinations.notes: No mandatory vaccinations for travelers from most countries.

healthInfo.waterNotes: Tap water is safe to drink throughout Portugal, though many people prefer the taste of bottled water (especially in the Algarve).
healthInfo.foodSafetyTips: Portuguese cuisine is delicious and generally safe. Bacalhau (salted cod) is a staple — safe from reputable restaurants. Fresh seafood, sardines, and grilled fish are excellent and safe. Pastéis de nata (egg tarts) from bakeries are safe. Be cautious with mayonnaise-based salads in hot weather.
sources: Portugal Ministry of Health (Ministério da Saúde)
healthInfo.medicalTourismNote: Portugal is emerging as a medical tourism destination for dental work, cosmetic surgery, and wellness retreats, combining quality healthcare with affordable living costs.

emergency.notes: 112 is the universal number. Operators speak English.

healthcare.costForTourists: EU citizens use EHIC. Non-EU: ER €50-200, private clinic €40-80. Public system is good but can have long waits. Private clinics are affordable by Western standards.
healthcare.pharmacyAccess: Pharmacies (farmácias) well-distributed. Pharmacists are knowledgeable. Some medications available without prescription that would require one elsewhere.
healthcare.hospitalNotes: Hospital da Luz and CUF in Lisbon are excellent private options. Public hospitals handle emergencies well. Algarve tourist areas have adequate facilities.
healthcare.insuranceAdvice: Travel insurance recommended for non-EU visitors.

controlledSubstances.note: Portugal decriminalized personal possession of all drugs in 2001. Possession of small amounts (10-day supply) is not criminal but may result in a referral to a 'dissuasion commission.' Trafficking remains illegal.

medications.generalAdvice: Portugal has progressive drug policies. However, don't mistake decriminalization for legalization — buying and selling is still illegal. Prescription medications: bring original packaging and prescriptions.

scams.name: Tuk-tuk overcharging
scams.description: Tuk-tuk drivers in Alfama and Bairro Alto charge €50-80 for short rides through the old town. No meters.
scams.avoidance: Agree on price before getting in. A 30-minute tour should be €20-30 max. Use Bolt or Uber for transportation instead.

scams.name: Drug dealers in Bairro Alto/Rossio
scams.description: Street dealers approach tourists offering drugs (often fake) in nightlife areas. Some work with pickpockets who steal from distracted buyers.
scams.avoidance: Ignore and walk away. Don't engage in conversation.

scams.name: Fake restaurant reviews luring tourists
scams.description: Restaurants near tourist sites with aggressive touts and inflated prices. Some have staff standing outside waving menus.
scams.avoidance: Avoid restaurants where someone is trying to pull you in from the street. Walk one block off the main tourist streets for better food and prices.

connectivity.simOptions: MEO, NOS, or Vodafone SIM at airports or stores. €10-15 for 30 days. eSIM via Airalo €5-8.
connectivity.wifiAvailability: Excellent free WiFi throughout Lisbon and Porto — cafes, restaurants, public spaces. Portugal has great internet infrastructure.
connectivity.bestOption: WiFi is so good in Portugal you might not need a SIM. eSIM as backup.

cultural.tipping: Not expected. Rounding up the bill or leaving 5-10% for good service is appreciated. No obligation.
cultural.dressCode: Casual. Cover shoulders at churches. Lisbon is hilly — wear comfortable shoes. Beachwear at the beach only.
cultural.greetings: Two cheek kisses for friends (women). Handshake for men. 'Olá' or 'Bom dia' (morning) / 'Boa tarde' (afternoon).
taboos: Comparing Portugal to Spain (they're proud of their distinct identity)
Speaking Spanish and assuming they'll understand (try Portuguese first)
cultural.haggling: Not common. Only at flea markets (Feira da Ladra in Lisbon).

safety.lgbtSafety: Same-sex marriage legal since 2010. Very tolerant. Lisbon has a growing LGBTQ+ scene.
safety.soloFemaleSafety: Very safe. One of the safest countries in Europe for solo female travelers.
safety.notes: Portugal is one of the safest countries in Europe. Petty theft exists in tourist areas of Lisbon (Tram 28, Bairro Alto) but violent crime is very rare.

practical.visaFreeCountries: US citizens: 90 days visa-free in Schengen area.
practical.bestTimeToVisit: April-October. Best weather June-September. Spring is beautiful and less crowded.
